title: Monitoring
blurb: Tests the three kinds of drift and how each shows up, PSI, KS and chi-squared tests, why input monitoring can't see concept drift, label lag, layered alert thresholds, and how to triage an alert before retraining.

ideas.title: KS and chi-squared tests at scale

questions.prompt: In the chapter's notation, what changes under data drift (covariate shift)?
options: Both P(X) and P(y | X) stay fixed, but the model's outputs change.
Only the label distribution P(y) changes.
P(X) changes while P(y | X) stays fixed.
P(y | X) changes while P(X) stays fixed.
questions.explanation: Data drift means the inputs look different but the relationship to the label hasn't moved. A change in P(y | X) is concept drift. A shift in outputs alone is prediction drift, which is a symptom, not a definition of either.

questions.prompt: Why can't concept drift be detected by watching the inputs alone?
options: Input monitoring only covers numeric features, and concept drift affects only categorical ones.
Concept drift happens too fast for input statistics to update.
The inputs can look completely normal. Only the mapping from inputs to outputs has changed.
Concept drift always comes with a broken pipeline, which hides the inputs.
questions.explanation: Under concept drift there is nothing to see in X. Detecting it needs ground-truth labels, usually lagged, or a strong proxy for correctness. Speed, feature type and pipeline bugs are not the reason.

questions.prompt: The share of transactions flagged as fraud doubles overnight. Which cause does the chapter say is very common in practice and worth checking first?
options: A model that retrained itself on the new traffic
A new fraud technique, since prediction drift always means concept drift
Seasonal shopping, since prediction drift always means data drift
A broken upstream feature pipeline sending nulls or default values
questions.explanation: Prediction drift is a symptom. It can come from data drift, concept drift, or, very often, a broken pipeline silently sending defaults. That is why the chapter says monitoring outputs often catches pipeline bugs faster than real drift. It doesn't always mean either kind of drift.

questions.prompt: A demand model was trained before a competitor cut prices. The same seasonal pattern no longer predicts the same sales. Which kind of drift is this, and what fixes it?
options: Data drift. Widening the training distribution to cover more seasons will fix it.
Concept drift. The old labels are no longer true, so it needs new labelled data.
Data drift. Resampling the existing training data to match current inputs will fix it.
Prediction drift. Recalibrating the output threshold will fix it.
questions.explanation: The inputs look the same but now map to different sales, so P(y | X) changed. The chapter says concept drift means the old labels are no longer even true, and no re-sampling of the old relationship will fix it. Widening or resampling the training data is a data-drift remedy.

questions.prompt: Using the chapter's thresholds, how should a PSI of 0.18 be read?
options: A confirmed performance drop that should trigger a retrain
A significant shift worth investigating
No significant shift
A moderate shift worth logging
questions.explanation: Below 0.10 is no significant shift, 0.10 to 0.25 is moderate and worth logging, and above 0.25 is significant and worth investigating. PSI measures input shift, so on its own it never confirms a performance drop.

questions.prompt: A feature has two buckets. The reference puts 50% of rows in each. Production puts 70% in the first and 30% in the second. What is the PSI? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: PSI = Σ (actual − expected) × ln(actual / expected) = (0.7 − 0.5) ln(0.7/0.5) + (0.3 − 0.5) ln(0.3/0.5) = 0.2 × 0.3365 + (−0.2)(−0.5108) = 0.0673 + 0.1022 = 0.169. Both terms are positive, which is always true for PSI.

questions.prompt: Four buckets each hold 25% of the reference. Production holds 10%, 20%, 30% and 40%. What is the PSI? Give three decimal places.
questions.explanation: The terms are (−0.15) ln(0.4) = 0.1374, (−0.05) ln(0.8) = 0.0112, (0.05) ln(1.2) = 0.0091 and (0.15) ln(1.6) = 0.0705. They sum to 0.228, a moderate shift just under the 0.25 line.

questions.prompt: Procedure 25.1 warns against computing bucket edges from the production sample. Why?
options: It makes PSI negative, which the thresholds don't cover.
Then the two sides no longer share buckets, so the PSI means nothing.
Production samples are too small to compute percentiles.
It makes the computation slower, because percentiles have to be found twice.
questions.explanation: PSI compares mass in matching buckets. Deciles of each sample put 10% in every bucket on both sides by construction, so a shift would vanish. The edges always come from the reference. PSI can't go negative, since each term is a difference times the log of the same ratio.

questions.prompt: What is the relationship between PSI and KL divergence, per the chapter?
options: PSI is the KL divergence computed on the model's output scores instead of on its input features.
PSI and KL divergence are unrelated. PSI comes from hypothesis testing.
PSI is the square root of KL divergence, which makes it a distance.
PSI is a symmetrised, discretised cousin of KL divergence, with the same log-ratio shape.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls PSI a symmetrised, discretised cousin of KL. In fact Σ (a − e) ln(a/e) equals KL(a‖e) + KL(e‖a) on the buckets. It is computed on inputs, comes from credit risk rather than hypothesis testing, and is not a square root.

questions.prompt: What does the KS statistic measure?
options: The difference between the two sample means, divided by the pooled standard deviation
The largest vertical gap between the two empirical cumulative distribution functions
The share of production values outside the training range
The sum of squared differences between bucket shares
questions.explanation: D = max over x of |F_expected(x) − F_actual(x)|. It is bounded between 0 and 1. The other options describe a standardised mean difference, a chi-squared-style sum, and a coverage check.

questions.prompt: A team's KS alert fires on every window now that traffic is 200,000 rows a day, even for shifts nobody cares about. What does the chapter recommend?
options: Lower the p-value threshold until the alerts stop.
Switch to the chi-squared test, which doesn't have this problem at large sample sizes.
Track the KS statistic as the main signal, and treat the p-value as information.
Downsample production to 100 rows so the p-value behaves.
questions.explanation: With large windows the p-value shrinks toward zero even for tiny, harmless shifts. The chapter says to use the statistic, an effect size, as the primary signal. Chi-squared has the same caveat at large samples. Throwing away data to fix a p-value hides real shifts too.

questions.prompt: A new plan_tier value launched last week shows up as significant drift in the chi-squared test. How does the chapter say to treat it?
options: As concept drift, which needs a retrain right away
As a bug in the chi-squared code, since unseen categories should always be dropped first
As a false alarm to suppress, since new categories always look significant
As a real, useful signal that the feature encoding needs to handle the new category
questions.explanation: The chapter says a brand-new category will always register as significant. That is often useful: the encoding pipeline has to deal with it. Listing 25.3 aligns unseen categories instead of dropping them for this reason. A new input category is a change in X, not evidence of concept drift.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter call performance monitoring inherently reactive?
options: It measures inputs, which change before the model does.
It only runs after a retrain, so it can't see the model that is serving right now.
Labels arrive late, so it shows past problems, not current ones.
It needs an alert from PSI before it can start.
questions.explanation: Label lag can be 60 to 90 days for chargebacks or 12 to 24 months for loan defaults. Performance monitoring is the gold standard because it measures real harm, but it confirms harm after the fact. That is why it is paired with fast input monitoring.

questions.prompt: Rolling accuracy looks steady, but the number of labelled rows per window has fallen by 80% over two weeks. What does Procedure 25.4 suggest?
options: Widen the window so the count looks normal again.
The label pipeline may be broken, leaving the monitor blind. Investigate it.
Retrain at once, because a fall in labelled rows means the model itself is failing.
Nothing. Steady accuracy means the model is fine.
questions.explanation: The procedure names this as a sign the monitor itself needs attention: metrics look fine while labelled feedback volume drops sharply. Steady accuracy on a shrinking, possibly biased sample proves little. Retraining doesn't fix a broken label feed.

questions.prompt: Accuracy drops sharply in only the most recent window. What should you check before reacting?
options: The model's training accuracy, since it may have been overfit
Whether the drop matches the PSI thresholds
The KS p-value for that window
The window's n, since the drop may only be a small-sample artefact
questions.explanation: rolling_performance records n per window for this reason. A recent window may have few labels so far, and a few errors swing the metric. The other checks don't tell you whether the drop is noise.

questions.prompt: Which retraining strategy can't catch concept drift on its own?
options: Performance-triggered retraining
Hybrid retraining
Retraining after a confirmed accuracy drop
Drift-triggered retraining
questions.explanation: Drift-triggered retraining fires on input statistics. Concept drift produces no input-side signal, so it never fires. Performance-triggered and hybrid strategies use labels, which do see concept drift, if late.

questions.prompt: Using classify in Listing 25.5, what is returned for max_psi = 0.40 and accuracy_drop = 0.02?
options: INVESTIGATE
RETRAIN
OK
LOG
questions.explanation: 0.02 is not above 0.05, so there is no confirmed drop and no RETRAIN. 0.40 is above PSI_ALERT (0.25), so the function returns INVESTIGATE before it reaches the LOG check.

questions.prompt: Using classify in Listing 25.5, what is returned for max_psi = 0.03 and accuracy_drop = 0.08?
options: RETRAIN
INVESTIGATE
LOG
OK
questions.explanation: The confirmed-drop check runs first. 0.08 > 0.05, so it returns RETRAIN, even though PSI is tiny. That ordering is deliberate: performance is the direct signal, and it is how concept drift gets caught.

questions.prompt: A PSI alert fires. Feature volume halved at the same moment, and many values are now null. What does the chapter's triage order say to do?
options: Lower the PSI threshold for that feature so the alert doesn't fire again.
Treat it as a pipeline bug. Fix the upstream source and don't retrain on it.
Treat it as real drift, and retrain on the new data.
Wait for a second window, then retrain if it persists.
questions.explanation: The first triage question is whether volume or nullness changed abruptly. If so, it is a pipeline bug, not drift: fix upstream. Retraining on broken inputs would teach the model the bug. Raising or lowering thresholds does not fix the source.

questions.prompt: Which of these does Procedure 25.5 recommend? Select all that apply.
options: Retrain automatically whenever PSI passes 0.25
Treat input drift with no accuracy drop as often needing no action
Require an alert to persist across two consecutive windows before paging
Alert on a steady upward trend in PSI, not only on the current value
questions.explanation: The procedure's rule of thumb is two consecutive windows before paging, plus trend alerts to catch drift that never crosses a threshold sharply. Its triage list says input drift without a performance drop often needs no action. Automatic retraining on PSI alone is what the hybrid pattern avoids.

questions.prompt: In the simulation, how did accuracy respond to the data drift in periods 3 and 4?
options: It rose sharply, because the shifted inputs were easier.
It barely moved, because the learned relationship still held there.
It collapsed below 0.3, because the model was extrapolating into new ground.
It fell steadily, from 0.78 to 0.60.
questions.explanation: Accuracy was 0.776 and 0.777 against about 0.77 to 0.78 in quiet weeks. The inputs moved by 0.8 and 1.4 standard deviations, but P(y | X) didn't change. The collapse to 0.254 came in period 5, the concept-drift period.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter call the core empirical result of its simulation?
options: The stable control feature x3 drifted in period 5, and that is what revealed the concept drift.
Data drift always hurts accuracy, so PSI is a reliable early warning of harm.
Input drift detection can't see concept drift. PSI flagged periods 3–4 and missed period 5.
PSI and KS disagree on which periods drifted, so both are needed.
questions.explanation: Period 5's PSI (0.016 and 0.021) looked like the quiet weeks, because the inputs never moved, yet accuracy fell to 0.254. A PSI-only monitor is backwards from where the harm was. x3 stayed flat throughout, and data drift in this simulation did not hurt accuracy.

questions.prompt: A team proposes retraining automatically whenever any feature's PSI passes 0.25. Using the simulation, what would that policy have done?
options: Retrained in periods 3–4 for nothing, and missed period 5, where the harm was.
Retrained in every period, because PSI stays above the 0.25 line in all six periods.
Retrained in periods 3–5, catching all the drift.
Retrained in period 5 only, which was correct.
questions.explanation: PSI passed 0.25 only in periods 3 and 4, where accuracy held. In period 5, max PSI was 0.021, so no retrain would fire, while accuracy had collapsed. The hybrid rule investigates on drift and retrains on confirmed performance drops, which is what Procedure 25.5 does.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in your own words why data drift and concept drift require fundamentally different detection strategies, using the $P(X)$ versus $P(y \mid X)$ formalism from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Data drift is a shift in $P(X)$ while $P(y \mid X)$ stays fixed. The inputs look different, but the rule mapping inputs to the true label hasn't changed. That means it's visible directly in the input features, with no need for a label at all. Comparing a reference sample of `x1` against a current sample and computing PSI or a KS statistic detects it immediately. Concept drift is the opposite. $P(y \mid X)$ itself changes, the same inputs now genuinely map to a different true output, which by construction leaves no trace in the marginal distribution of $X$. There is nothing unusual to see in the inputs, because nothing about the inputs changed. Only the relationship changed, and the only way to observe a broken relationship is to compare predictions against actual outcomes, i.e. labels. This is why the two failure modes need different detection machinery: PSI/KS on features for data drift, and rolling performance metrics against ground truth (with whatever label lag that entails) for concept drift. One can't substitute for the other, because they're measuring genuinely different quantities.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the worked example's period 3-4 results, explain why a monitoring system relying only on accuracy would have missed the input drift that PSI caught clearly.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: In periods 3-4, accuracy moved only trivially: 0.776 and 0.777, essentially indistinguishable from the quiet-period baseline of ~0.76-0.78, even though `x1` and `x2` shifted by 0.8 and then 1.4 standard deviations. A monitoring system that only tracked accuracy would have seen nothing worth flagging across those two periods, because the model's learned relationship still held even as it extrapolated into a less-familiar region of feature space. The substantial input shift caused no proportional harm to predictive performance. PSI, by contrast, is computed directly from the input distributions and doesn't need performance to move to register a signal. It caught the shift immediately and dramatically (0.736 and 0.640 in period 3, climbing to 1.878 and 1.935 in period 4), well before there was any accuracy-based reason for concern. This is exactly the leading-indicator property the Exposition describes. Data drift is detectable before, or even in the complete absence of, a performance impact, which an accuracy-only monitor is structurally unable to see.

bookExercises.prompt: Reproduce Listing 25.1's logic on period 5's `x1` feature against the period 0 reference. Given that the resulting PSI is near zero, explain in one sentence why this is exactly what the tutorial's design predicts rather than a detection failure.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Running Listing 25.1 with period 0's `x1` values as `expected` and period 5's `x1` values as `actual` reproduces the table's reported value of 0.016, essentially the same order of magnitude as the quiet-period noise floor (0.021, 0.028 in periods 1-2), and nowhere close to the 0.10 "moderate shift" threshold. This is exactly what the tutorial's design predicts, not a detection failure, because period 5 was constructed to leave the input distribution of `x1` completely untouched. Only the sign of the coefficient relating `x1` to the label was flipped. Since PSI is a function purely of the two `x1` samples' bucketed distributions, and those distributions are statistically identical between period 0 and period 5 by construction, a near-zero PSI is the correct, expected output. The tool is doing exactly what it's supposed to do: reporting that the inputs didn't move, which is true.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Procedure 25.5's `classify` function with `PSI_ALERT=0.25` and `ACCURACY_DROP_RETRAIN=0.05`, determine the decision for a hypothetical period with `max_psi=0.30` and `accuracy_drop=0.02`, and explain why that decision is the conservative choice rather than an aggressive one.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Walking `max_psi=0.30, accuracy_drop=0.02` through Listing 25.5's `classify` function: the first check, `accuracy_drop > ACCURACY_DROP_RETRAIN` (0.02 > 0.05), is false, so it does not return `'RETRAIN'`. The second check, `max_psi > PSI_ALERT` (0.30 > 0.25), is true, so the function returns `'INVESTIGATE'`. This is the conservative choice rather than the aggressive one, because PSI alone, even a fairly large PSI of 0.30, is only an indirect proxy for drift, per the Trade-offs table, and the accuracy drop of 0.02 is well under the 0.05 threshold that would confirm real harm. Retraining is expensive and carries its own risk (a new model version that could behave worse), so the decision rule deliberately withholds that action until performance evidence confirms the input shift actually mattered. This exactly mirrors what happened with periods 3-4 in the Worked Example: elevated PSI, unconfirmed performance impact, `INVESTIGATE` rather than `RETRAIN`.

bookExercises.prompt: A customer's fraud model shows PSI of 0.4 on the `transaction_amount` feature this week, with no confirmed labels yet due to a 60-day chargeback lag. Using this chapter's triage checklist, list the two most likely explanations you'd rule out before recommending a retrain.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Per this chapter's triage checklist, two explanations should be ruled out before recommending a retrain. First, a pipeline bug rather than real drift. Check whether `transaction_amount`'s volume or null rate changed abruptly around the same time the PSI spike appeared, since a broken upstream feature source (a currency conversion step failing, a new payment provider sending amounts in a different unit) can produce a large PSI reading that has nothing to do with genuine customer behaviour change. Second, whether the shift coincides with a known, already-understood business event: a product launch, a new merchant category going live, a marketing campaign driving a different customer mix. In that case the drift is real but expected, and doesn't by itself indicate the model's *relationship* between transaction amount and fraud has broken, only that the input distribution has moved into a region the model may or may not still generalise well to. Only after ruling out both would input drift alone, still without confirmed labels, justify escalating past `INVESTIGATE`.

bookExercises.prompt: Propose a business-metric proxy (not a model metric) that a team could monitor to catch concept drift faster than waiting for the full label lag, for a churn model where "did they actually churn" isn't known for 30 days. State one risk of relying on your proposed proxy.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A usable proxy is early engagement decline: a drop in login frequency, feature usage, or session count over a short rolling window (7-14 days) relative to each customer's own recent baseline, monitored as an aggregate rate across the customer base rather than waiting for the 30-day confirmed-churn label. If the proxy's population-level rate shifts meaningfully compared to its historical range, that's a much faster signal that *something* about customer behaviour or the product experience has changed than waiting a full month for confirmed churn outcomes. The risk: engagement decline is a proxy, not the label itself, and the relationship between "engagement dropped" and "customer actually churned" can itself drift. A seasonal dip (e.g. a product used mainly during a school term going quiet over summer) could trigger the proxy without any actual increase in churn, producing a false alarm and, if acted on by retraining, potentially degrading the model on a false premise rather than a real one.

bookExercises.prompt: The chapter notes that a brand-new category appearing in a categorical feature always registers as chi-squared drift. Research (or reason from the formula) whether the same is true for PSI on a numeric feature when production values fall entirely outside the reference distribution's range, and explain what the `compute_psi` implementation in Listing 25.1 does in that case.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer. Reasoning from Listing 25.1's implementation: bucket edges are computed once, from `expected`'s percentiles (`np.unique(np.percentile(expected, breakpoints))`), and then `np.histogram(actual, edges)` is used to bin the current sample into those same, fixed edges. `np.histogram` places any value below the first edge or above the last edge into neither bin. Those out-of-range values simply don't get counted in `actual_counts` at all, rather than being forced into the nearest bucket. If production values fall entirely outside the reference range, the extreme buckets nearest that edge would show `actual_pct` collapsing toward the zero-replacement floor (`1e-4`) while whichever bucket happens to still catch some mass dominates. If *all* actual values fall outside every bucket edge, every `actual_counts` bin is zero, `actual_counts.sum()` is zero, and `actual_pct = actual_counts / actual_counts.sum()` divides by zero, producing NaNs rather than a large, meaningful PSI. That's a real gap in the implementation, since the case that most obviously represents a severe drift (production data occupying a completely different range) is exactly where the function is likely to break rather than report a maximal score. Contrast this with chi-squared for categorical data, which explicitly reindexes and fills unseen categories with a small floor value rather than silently dropping them. The numeric PSI implementation would benefit from an analogous explicit clamp of out-of-range values into the nearest edge bucket, instead of dropping them from the histogram.
